title: Chapter 78 — The Psychology of Pricing and Value
intro: Anchors, framing, value construction, and the fairness instinct that drives how customers evaluate price.

sections.title: Price Is Relative
sections.content:
A $3,000 refrigerator feels expensive until you compare it to a $5,000 refrigerator. Then it feels like a deal.

Anchoring is the principle that the first number a customer hears sets the frame for everything that follows. This is why the recommendation sequence matters. If you show the premium option first and then show the mid-range option, the mid-range feels affordable. If you show the budget option first and then show the mid-range, the mid-range feels expensive.

The product did not change. The frame changed.

sections.title: Value Is Built — Not Claimed
sections.content:
You cannot just say 'this is a great value.' You have to build it.

Value is built through discovery — understanding what matters to the customer. Value is built through the demo — showing them how features connect to their life. Value is built through the complete ticket — showing everything included.

By the time you present the price, the customer should already understand what they are getting and why it is worth it. If you have to convince them of the value after presenting the price, you presented the price too early.

sections.title: The Fairness Instinct
sections.content:
Customers do not just evaluate whether a price is high or low. They evaluate whether it is fair. Fair pricing means transparency, consistency, and a clear connection between what they pay and what they get.

Never surprise a customer with hidden fees. Never offer different prices to different customers for the same product. Never make the customer feel like they are being taken advantage of.

The fairness instinct is powerful. A customer who feels the price is fair will buy — even if it is higher than a competitor. A customer who feels the price is unfair will walk — even if it is actually a good deal.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating pricing psychology, ask:

Does the salesperson build value before presenting price — or lead with the number?
Do they use anchoring effectively in their recommendation sequence?
Do they maintain pricing transparency and consistency?
Does the customer perceive the price as fair by the time the close arrives?
